title: What the Protestants mean by the grace of Christ
source_text: XXIII. Caeterum in hac quaestione, gratiae Christi nomine non dignantur auxilia illa ordinis naturalis quae Deus non denegat infidelibus ipsis in infidelitate sua permanentibus: Sed gratiam Christi vocant eam duntaxat quae incipit a fide, & ea non qualicunque, verum Christiana & divinitus infusa, quaeque iners & mortua non sit, sed quae per dilectionem operari incipiat.
pass_a_gloss: XXIII. But in this question, with the name of the grace of Christ they do not honour those helps of the natural order which God does not deny to unbelievers themselves remaining in their unbelief: But the grace of Christ they call that only which begins from faith, and that not of whatever kind, but Christian and divinely infused, and which is not inert and dead, but which through love begins to work.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXIII. In this question, however, they do not give the name 'grace of Christ' to the helps of the natural order that God does not refuse even to unbelievers who remain in their unbelief.

They call grace of Christ only the grace that begins with faith, and not with faith of just any kind, but with Christian faith infused by God, which is not idle and dead but begins to work through love.

lemmas.gloss: those helps of the natural order

lemmas.latin: eam duntaxat quae incipit a fide
lemmas.gloss: that only which begins from faith
and which is not inert and dead

choices.why: For the Protestants of this Part the saving grace that begins with faith, as distinct from the 'special help' of providence that restrains the unregenerate.
